title: Om mani padme hum
hook: six syllables, spun in prayer wheels and carved into stones along mountain paths

segments.voice: Yesterday, lamrim, the staircase of the path. Your line was precious human life. What opening did you name that you didn't have to earn? Today, a sound that Tibetan Buddhists send out into the world. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

A brass cylinder the size of a coffee can, set on a handle. An older woman walks around a temple, turning it with a small flick of the wrist, clockwise, again and again, while her lips move. Along the path outside, flat stones are stacked into walls, and each one is carved with the same row of letters. Up on the ridge, prayer flags carry them too. Inside the cylinder, tightly rolled, is paper printed over and over with those same letters. The whole landscape seems to be saying one sentence. Six syllables that Tibetan Buddhists tie to compassion. Today's word is that sentence.
screen: `A WHEEL TURNED CLOCKWISE.` → `STONES CARVED ALONG THE PATH.` → `ONE SENTENCE, EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Om mani padme hum is a mantra, a sacred sound to be repeated. Four turns. First, whose sound it is. Tibetan Buddhists connect it with Avalokiteshvara, called Chenrezig in Tibetan, the bodhisattva of compassion, the one who hears the cries of the world. A Mahayana scripture, the Karandavyuha Sutra, praises the mantra at length. To say it is to turn the mind toward that compassion. Second, the words. Mani is a jewel. Padma is a lotus. So a common English rendering is your line: the jewel in the lotus. That's a start, though not a settled one. Scholars argue over the grammar, and Tibetan teachers often skip the translation altogether and explain the syllables one at a time, each linked to a quality to cultivate or a kind of suffering to be freed from. Third, the wheel and the stone. In Tibetan practice the mantra isn't only spoken. Written inside a prayer wheel, it's said to be sent out with every turn. Carved on a stone, it stays there for every passerby. Printed on a flag, the wind carries it. The idea is that compassion shouldn't depend on one person remembering to say it. Fourth, the jewel and the lotus as a picture. The lotus grows up out of mud and opens clean. Teachers use it as an image of a mind that stays open in a messy world. The jewel is something precious that was there all along. You don't need to settle the grammar to hold both pictures.
screen: `THE SOUND OF COMPASSION.` · `JEWEL, LOTUS, AND A GRAMMAR DEBATE.` · `SPUN, CARVED, CARRIED BY WIND.` · `A LOTUS OUT OF MUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear it. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. If you'd like, say the mantra softly, om mani padme hum, at an easy, steady pace, the way it's said in Tibetan homes and temples. If saying it doesn't fit you, just listen to it inwardly, or simply rest with the breath and the picture of a lotus opening above muddy water. There's nothing to achieve. Let the sound, or the quiet, do the work. The bell holds the time.
Om mani padme hum. The mantra of compassion in Tibetan Buddhism, linked to Chenrezig, spun in wheels and carved in stone. Often rendered the jewel in the lotus. Today's word.

Your line: the jewel in the lotus. Today, find a recording of the mantra chanted by Tibetan monks or nuns, and listen to it once, all the way through, doing nothing else. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists often recite om mani padme hum on prayer beads, turn prayer wheels that contain it, and carve or print it on stones and flags, as an expression of the compassion of Chenrezig.
